clue.text: Father Inge has been terribly well: an advantage, incidentally

parts.note: FR is the standard abbreviation for Father, a priest's title

indicators.note: terribly suggests the letters of the word been are thrown into disorder

parts.note: to be well is to be fit and healthy

explanation.surface: Dean Inge, the famous cleric, has been in excellent health, which is a handy bonus.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terribly' turns BEEN into BENE. William Inge was a well-known Dean of St Paul's, which makes 'Father Inge' look like one person.
explanation.definitionFit: A perk given alongside salary is an extra advantage that comes incidentally with a job.

clue.text: His adored would burn his offerings?

definitions.text: His adored would burn his offerings?

parts.words: His adored would burn his offerings?
parts.note: the object of his devotion is a flame, so anything laid before it as an offering would be consumed

explanation.surface: A devotee whose beloved would burn up any gift he brought.
explanation.definitionFit: A Zoroastrian-style devotee venerates flame, the thing that burns offerings.

clue.text: One wise man's representation

parts.note: the Roman numeral I stands for one
a mage is a learned man or magus, like the Magi

explanation.surface: A picture of one of the Three Wise Men.
explanation.definitionFit: A likeness or picture is a representation of something.

clue.text: Michaelmas diet gives me skin-trouble.

explanation.surface: Eating the traditional autumn feast leaves me with a skin complaint.
explanation.walkthrough: Michaelmas (29 September) is traditionally celebrated in Britain with a roast goose; 'gives me' only links the two senses.
explanation.definitionFit: The meat of the bird eaten at Michaelmas, and also the bumpy skin raised by cold or fear.

clue.text: This one repatriated Tommy

parts.note: a 'one' here is a First World War slang wound serious enough to send a British soldier home to England

explanation.surface: A soldier was sent home by a particular wound.
explanation.walkthrough: Tommy is a British private soldier; a wound bad enough to ship him home to Britain was called a '— one' after the slang name for home.
explanation.definitionFit: Soldiers' slang for Britain gave its name to a homeward-sending wound in the trenches.

clue.text: Denies being seen returning holding a gun

indicators.note: holding means one piece wraps round and contains the other
returning means the word seen is read backwards

parts.note: a gat is American slang for a gun

explanation.surface: Someone refuses to admit they were spotted coming back with a weapon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' turns SEEN into NEES, which is split by GAT.
explanation.definitionFit: To contradict or nullify a claim is to deny it.

clue.text: Old Foreign Office addendum on dandies

parts.note: FO is the abbreviation for the former Foreign Office
PS, a postscript, is something added at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: An addition to a dispatch from the Foreign Office concerning fashionable men.
explanation.definitionFit: Men vain about their clothes are fops, synonyms for dandies.

clue.text: Summit meeting in Paris ?

parts.note: in French the summit of the body is the head, so heads meeting heads is a private talk

explanation.surface: A high-level diplomatic conference held in the French capital.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase means head to head, a private conversation between two people.

clue.text: But not a round robin

parts.note: a round robin is a letter sent to many people; this one is round only in being circulated, not a bird

explanation.surface: An object is shaped like a ring yet is no plump bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A letter sent round to many recipients is the formal name for a round robin.

clue.text: Argument about gains on 'change

parts.note: re means about or concerning

indicators.note: 'change, short for exchange, signals the letters of gains on are exchanged around

explanation.surface: A debate over profits made on the Stock Exchange.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change, with an apostrophe, is the old name for the Stock Exchange, so 'gains on 'change' reads as market profits. As the anagram signal it rearranges GAINSON into ASONING.
explanation.definitionFit: Logical argument is a process of reasoning towards a conclusion.

clue.text: Make Gilbert's little maid sing out in the palace

indicators.note: out tells us that the word sing is taken away from the name

parts.note: Pitti-Sing is one of the three little maids in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Mikado

explanation.surface: Get a character from The Mikado to perform a song in a royal residence.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pitti is a famous Renaissance palace in Florence, now an art gallery.

clue.text: A question of location

parts.note: the interrogative word one uses to ask about a place

explanation.surface: A query about where something is.
explanation.definitionFit: The interrogative asking which place something is in.

clue.text: Strikes are great successes

explanation.surface: Industrial action turns out to be a triumph.
explanation.definitionFit: Blows landed are strikes, and big popular triumphs are smashes, such as chart toppers.

clue.text: No parson is left a single hundred

parts.note: I, the Roman numeral one, gives single
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: A clergyman is left with just one hundred.
explanation.definitionFit: Lay rather than clerical, describing someone outside the clergy.

clue.text: Sort of fit to accept it, Al ? Possibly

indicators.note: possibly suggests the letters of accept it Al could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Asking a man called Al whether he is fit enough to take something on.
explanation.definitionFit: Catalepsy brings a trance-like seizure, so the adjective describes that kind of fit.

clue.text: Reginald is on our side, in splendid form

parts.note: Reg is the usual short form of the name Reginald
an ally is someone on our side

explanation.surface: Reginald supports us and is looking magnificent.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something royally means doing it with splendour and pomp.

clue.text: Port security unit protects joint

parts.note: to guard is to protect
the hip is a joint of the body

explanation.surface: A harbour safety team watches over a shared venture.
explanation.definitionFit: A warship stationed to protect a harbour is a naval security unit for a port.

clue.text: Lake pike appears high

parts.note: a pike in the Lake District is a peak, and this one is among England's highest

explanation.surface: A big fish in a lake leaps up out of the water.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Lake District 'pike' means a peak; Scafell and Scafell Pike are England's highest mountains, in Cumbria.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cumbrian mountain beside England's highest peak, Scafell Pike, in the Lakes.

clue.text: Apprehends audible agreement — but it's only a rumour

parts.note: to apprehend a sound is to hear it

indicators.note: audible means the word for agreement is taken as it sounds when spoken

parts.note: aye is a word of agreement, as in a vote

explanation.surface: Someone catches a spoken yes, yet suspects it is mere gossip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'audible' turns AYE into its sound-alike AY.
explanation.definitionFit: Unverified information passed by word of mouth is gossip, only a rumour.

clue.text: Yet we're perhaps in grave circumstances

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters of yet we're might be rearranged

explanation.surface: Even so, we may be in a serious situation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges YETWERE. 'Grave circumstances' means surroundings of graves: the tree is a churchyard fixture.
explanation.definitionFit: Yews are traditionally planted in churchyards, surrounded by burial plots.

clue.text: Wherewith an adder makes a bad auditor

definitions.text: Wherewith an adder makes a bad auditor

parts.words: Wherewith an adder makes a bad auditor
parts.note: an adder is a snake, and the deaf adder of Psalm 58 will not listen; an auditor here is a listener

explanation.surface: A careless accountant who adds figures badly makes a poor inspector of books.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Adder' and 'auditor' suggest bookkeeping, but the adder is the snake that stops its ears in Psalm 58, and an auditor is a listener.
explanation.definitionFit: Turning an unhearing organ to someone means refusing to listen, like the deaf adder.

clue.text: Climb down the family tree?

parts.note: to go down a genealogy is to be a later generation, as well as simply going down

explanation.surface: Clambering down from the tree the family owns.
explanation.definitionFit: To go downwards, and to come from an ancestor, are both meanings of this verb.

clue.text: Rooms for 'Batman ?

explanation.surface: Lodgings for the caped crusader.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Batman' looks like the comic hero; read it as 'bat man', a batter at cricket, who straps on leg guards.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang for living quarters, and the leg guards a cricket batter wears.

clue.text: Soundly treat the sheep

indicators.note: soundly signals that the word meaning treat is replaced by one sounding the same

parts.note: to use someone is to treat them in a certain way

explanation.surface: Give the flock a proper, thorough treatment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soundly' looks like 'thoroughly' but asks for a sound-alike of USE.
explanation.definitionFit: Female sheep are ewes; the plural matches 'the sheep' taken as many.

clue.text: Give the slip to 'David, returning East

indicators.note: returning tells us that the short name is read backwards

parts.note: Dave is a familiar short form of David

explanation.surface: Escaping from David as he comes back from the east.
explanation.definitionFit: To escape or elude someone is to give them the slip.

clue.text: An old-fashioned tip may be helpful

parts.note: an gives the single letter A
vail is an archaic word for a gratuity or tip

explanation.surface: An outdated piece of advice could still come in handy.
explanation.walkthrough: VAIL is an old word for a tip given to servants; 'tip' looks like advice.
explanation.definitionFit: To avail is to be of use, to help or benefit.

clue.text: Rabbit booked, about to enter railway

indicators.note: to enter means the second piece goes inside the first

parts.note: BR is the abbreviation for British Rail, the old national railway
re means about or concerning

explanation.surface: A rabbit has a reservation and is about to board a train.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rabbit booked' is the rabbit of books: Brer Rabbit from the Uncle Remus stories.
explanation.definitionFit: The title Brother in the Uncle Remus tales, borne by the storybook rabbit.

clue.text: Comes from The Gables, her place in Surrey.

indicators.note: comes from signals the letters are taken from within the words that follow

explanation.surface: A woman lives at a house called The Gables, her Surrey home.
explanation.definitionFit: A town in the county of Surrey, near Kingston.

clue.text: A double rent repaired in the fortifications

indicators.note: repaired suggests the letters of the pieces are put back together in a new order
double means the word rent is written twice

explanation.surface: A tear twice over is mended in the castle walls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'double' makes RENTRENT; with A, 'repaired' rearranges ARENTRENT.
explanation.definitionFit: An inward-pointing angle in a line of defences is a feature found in the fortifications.

clue.text: Erect buildings in this style

explanation.surface: Put up structures in a particular architectural manner.
explanation.definitionFit: Upright, standing vertical; also the late English Gothic architectural style.
